units.text: Development and experimental studies of a light vehicle diesel after treatment system with DOC, DPF and urea SCR
Introduction

Compliance with BS VI and Euro VI standards is necessary to achieve stringent reductions in emissions from traditional diesel engines, including carbon monoxide (CO), hydrocarbons (HC), soot, and nitrogen oxides (NOx).The employment of diesel catalyst (DOC), diesel particulate IOP Publishing doi:10.1088/1742-6596/2925/1/012008 2 filters (DPFs), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR) systems is becoming common in diesel engines used in light vehicles, medium-duty engines, big locomotives, and marine applications.[1].One important factor is that the present light-vehicle applications' cost, packaging issues, and technical complexity will surpass those of three-way converters [2].The design process includes the whole system architecture and packaging, the objectives related to back pressure and pollutants, and the anticipated efficiency of the SCR system.Diesel oxidation catalysts (DOC) and catalytic particulate filters (CDPF) with motor heating and control systems for active regeneration are generally utilized in light automobiles to reduce hydrocarbons (HC), carbon monoxide (CO), and soot formation.Nitrogen dioxide (NO2), along with hydroxide (OH), reacts with water vapour to form nitrogenic acid and is the primary cause of acid rain in the atmosphere.Profound respiratory symptoms are induced by nitrogen dioxide (NO2) intake, including bronchitis and asthma lung infection [4].Clear evidence indicates that the presence of NO2 will result in early mortality from cardiovascular and respiratory causes.The rise in automobile and power station emissions, accounting for around 40 percent of smog, is another consequence of NOx pollution in metropolitan areas [5].Applying treatment to exhaust gas is the most straightforward method to reduce emissions without altering the engine, operating conditions, or fuel, and it will comply with stringent regulatory standards [6].The architects of the SCR system have gained a significant reputation due to the system's crucial role in reducing emissions.Over the last five years, there has been significant production of diesel engines after treatment methods [7,8].An essential consideration is that the production of NOx and other pollutants is vertically proportional when diesel/biodiesel is used as a fuel.The use of selective catalytic reduction (SCR) in diesel/biodiesel mixed engines effectively reduces NOx emissions without modifying any motor design [9].Solid-state catalytic reduction (SCR) reduces the catalytic environment of a certain component.The SCR technique aims to decrease the carbon emissions stemming from NOx by converting them into nitrogen (N2).This process transforms ammonia vapours (NH3) into ecologically benign nitrogen (N2) and water (H2O) for the catalytic site, which is required for the removal of hazardous NOx emissions.The main constituents of NOx are NO and NO2, with each component at a proportion of around 90% and 10%, respectively.The conversion of NO2 to N2 is considered a slow reaction, whereas the conversion of NO2 to N2 is identified as a rapid process [10,11].However, when considering the test restrictions, indirect methods such as the combination of NOx reduction and slip ammonia [12] and the NOx ammonia ratio (feed ratio) are used to assess the mixture's effectiveness.In technical terms, the homogeneity of pre-SCR ammonia is preferred [13].A novel catalytic oxidation granular bed device, consisting of an Earth's molecular sieve, has been developed to enhance DOC + DPF + SCR technology for diesel engine reprocessing.This highly effective device allows CO and CH to oxidize and remove tiny PM Particles, replacing the prior DOC + DPF mode.The device was mounted at the exhaust discharge of the diesel engine, significantly improving the cleanliness of thin-carbonized diesel exhaust when subjected to the SCR catalytic reduction system after its passage through the pretreatment unit.[19,20].The urea system is the primary element of the denitrification technology of the SCR system.To mitigate excessive ammonia spraying leading to 'ammonia escape' and enhance NOx conversion efficiency, it is necessary to monitor the amount of urea injection.This monitoring is a crucial responsibility that ensures the system's optimal performance.The production of urine deposits may lead to backpressure, energy dissipation, and material deterioration, contingent upon the inadequate evaporation of the urea solution.The main scope and objectives of the research are to control and reduce the emissions from stationary diesel engines.The injection of urea vapour soot and unburned HC and CO are reduced to about 90%.A reduced reagent (ammonia) CFD goal is provided, acknowledging that existing CFD spray modelling often underestimates uniformity compared to empirical testing due to the constraints of CFD mathematical formulations.DOC, DPF, and SCR technologies enable substantial noise reduction via the very porous structures located downstream of the engine, rendering a muffler unnecessary for this system.
Control Strategy of SCR

Urea is the recommended reducing agent for toxicological and security concerns in SCR applications.A solution of aqueous urea is injected into the hot exhaust gas upstream of the SCR catalyst.Before the SCR Reaction, urea is broken down into carbon dioxide and ammonia [19].The first step is to evaporate the water from the droplets, which turns the liquid urea in Eq. ( 1) into solid or molten urea.

NH2-CO-NH2 (molten) → NH3 (gas) + HNCO (gas) (2) Equimolar quantities are thus composed of ammonia and isocyanic acid.Isocyanic acid is very stable during the gas phase but readily hydrolyzes with a large number of solid oxides, reacting with water vapour Eq. Experimental Procedures
Experimental Setup

An engine testing facility researched concept gaseous urea dosing systems on a Kirloskar single-cylinder four-stroke vertical water-cooled compression ignition engine.The exhaust line consisted of a diesel oxidation catalyst (DOC), a diesel particle filter (DPF) similar to those used in the tested engine, and an Al2O3-TiO2 SCR catalyst combined with a urea-dosing system for development.The dosing system of the AVL DI gas 444N five gas-analyzer with NOx sensors was used, and Apex Innovations Pvt Ltd.Enginesoft designed the automation programme is a proprietary technology package developed by Apex Specialising in Labview for monitoring engine performance.The primary process included preheating and letting the urea water solution (UWS) evaporate in a specific chamber before applying the exhaust gas directly to the SCR intake.The procedure for the given after-treatment system is shown in Figure 1.

The testing equipment and technical specifications are shown in Table 1.This experiment used the Kirloskar TV1 engine, which had a maximum power output of 5.2 kW, a rated speed of 1500 rpm, and a maximum torque of 1460 N-m.Five exhaust gas analysers evaluate exhaust emissions without a vehicle load and calculate transient pollution in both partial and full load scenarios for diesel-powered vehicles.The chemical composition of HC, CO, CO2, O2, and NOx mainly determines combustion emissions from engine exhaust.The detailed specifications of the AVL DI GAS 444N five gas analyser may be found in Table 2.

The two measurements obtained from the AVL smoke metre 437°C, which demonstrate the properties of opacity and light absorption, underscore the precision of this instrument.It is a reliable experimental tool for investigating free acceleration and transient behaviour.The  device's measurement range is from 0% to 100% with an accuracy of ±1% of the whole scale and a resolution of 0.1%.The refractive index spans from 0 to 99.99 m -1 with an accuracy above ±0.1 m-1 and a resolution of 0.01 m -1 .With an engine speed ranging from 400 to 6000 rpm, it provides accurate and detailed data.

A tubular reactor, seen as the SCR catalyst, is pivotal in reducing NOx emissions from diesel gas exhaust.The arrangement of this reactor, consisting of many narrow channels, significantly enhances the efficiency of catalytic surface transfers.In its vapour state, Urea is pumped at the reactor intake, where it undergoes conversion to NH3 and subsequent deposition in the active catalyst phase.The stored NH3 then undergoes catalytic chemical reactions with NOx.This review underscores the crucial role of NH3 storage in controlling the decrease of NOx, highlighting the significance of the SCR catalyst in emissions control.

The active surface of the SCR adsorbs NH3 in the gas treatment process.The adsorbed NH3 is not capable of being absorbed by the substratum.The coverage ratio is the ratio of the number of catalytic sites occupied to the total number.It is the coverage ratio.Advanced modelling and measurement efforts are necessary to study the dynamic dynamics of adsorption and desorption.They lie much beyond the current scope of our research.The absence of direct oxidation of adsorbed NH3 by oxygen is explained by its lack of impact on closed-loop analyses.

Therefore, the transition process is straightforward and easily manageable.The adsorbed NH3 undergoes a reaction with nitrogen and water via the use of NOx.The cumulative nitrogen oxides (NOx) in this sample are NO and NO2.Control is exercised over the system under temporary situations, effectively managing fluctuations in the exhaust gas stream, temperature, and NOx concentration.

The desired urea-mass value was calculated for both open and closed transfer functions.The urea injection was adjusted in the open-loop control, and the α-ratio was adjusted in the closed-loop model.The control unit computed the physical exhaust mass flow rate and the NOx value obtained from the portable NOx sensor.By the design of the dosing system, the Urea was supplied at a pressure of about 2 bar to either the exhaust gas stream or the heating chamber.

The quantity of Urea dosed was determined by calculating the ratio of ammonia molecules produced by the reduction agent (NH3) to nitrogen oxide (NOx) created in the main flow of the exhaust gas (α = NH3/NOx).

Measurements of the exhaust emission, gas temperature, and ammonia content were taken, which were continually available upstream of the DOC and downstream of the SCR.An AVL 437:C measuring instrument equipped with an automated ammonia analyser with an accuracy of ± 1% was installed on the emission testing bench.The rate of urea flow injection was indicated in milligrams per second.
Measurement Methods

The crucial phase of the study was conducted in the steady state engine state.A comprehensive study methodology has been devised to include various exhaust gas temperatures.The concept and traditional urea-dosing methods were used to assess their respective performance.The gas temperature at the split-cycle reactor (SCR) input ranged from 180°C to 380°C, with each phase rising by about 40°C from 180°C.The driving speeds were set at a constant 1500 revolutions per minute (rpm), while the fuel temperature was controlled by adjusting the engine load within the range of 60 to 400 Nm.During testing, the EGR valve was deactivated, resulting in the reduction of NOx emissions.Concentrations of raw gas ranged from The exhaust composition of the diesel engine exhibited a strong correlation with active operating circumstances.This study used the eddy current dynamometer to evaluate the operational condition of the diesel engine.The fuel exhaust composition was determined using the AVL DI gas 444N five-gas analyser with NOx sensors.Emission components such as CO, HC, CO2, NOx, and others may be calculated from the exhaust gas.This selenium photocell sensor is used to quantify the concentration of NOx.

Passing through the measured gas, the gas molecules absorb the light of a certain wavelength, and this relationship adheres to the absorption law of Lambert-Beer.The measured gas is conveyed into the measuring chamber using the sample pump.After the light sensor and AC output signal detect the light, the measurement and control device obtains a gas concentration value based on the DC signal.The control system can display the magnitude of the gas concentration to a temperature sensor using digital filtering and linear interpolation software.
The test operating conditions implemented were: 1. Constant speed and idle load.2. At a constant speed, the load is varied in four cases: 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%, and so on.
Based on the five operating conditions, the first experiment compared the various NOx concentrations between the integrated catalytic unit and traditional equipment under multiple settings.

Subsequently, detailed information on the effectiveness of NOx conversion using the optimised catalytic bed system with SCR after-processing system was provided.Additionally, measurements were taken for speed, torque, power consumption, gasoline, oil, exhaust temperature and pressure, input and output water temperature, upstream and downstream SCR system NOx, and other particular temperature and pressure sensor data.The enhanced catalytic unit implements the urea injection technique and NOx reduction approach.Finally, the gas was sent to the AVL smoke metre.The gas opacity and absorption phenomena were investigated.The experimental arrangement is shown in Figure 2.
Practical Implementation

Examining the test findings explores the possible use of the gaseous urea concept.Utilising selective catalytic reduction (SCR), researchers are now investigating the possibility of administering NOx reduction agents in the gas phase as a possible method to reduce problems associated with inefficient urea evaporation, the conversion of ammonia and urea, and the process of deposit formation at low gas temperatures.

Urea heating and evaporation were initiated by applying electric energy at a power of 200 W. Nevertheless, it is important to link it with the management of the urea stream for optimal results.At that time, the power level was appropriate for evaporating water into a urea solution.Furthermore, urea is introduced into the gas stream using a mixing device due to increased back pressure.It is necessary to optimise and overhaul the mixing component.

The characteristics of the material formed by the mixing catalyst play a pivotal role in influencing the rate at which thermal urea breaks down.By strategically selecting materials, we can potentially enhance the conversion of urea to ammonia.Furthermore, there are modifications to the initial setup of the gaseous urea system.Notably, the formation of a robust urea deposit inside the heating chamber at certain phases of the engine is a significant development.
Results and Discussions

The test included the idle load and speed from the overall working circumstances and the work conditions of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% intensity.Each standard emission point was designated at each normal operation stage to inject urea and study the efficiency of NOx conversion using a modified device.The test results were sequentially shown in Figures 3 to 7.
Carbon Monoxide (CO) Emissions

The level of unsaturation, type of fuel, cylinder temperature, C/H ratio, and incomplete combustion all substantially influence the production of CO.The CO emissions for the SCR and DOC+DPF setups were 0.038 and 0.017 lower than the standard setup (0.039), respectively.However, the SCR and DOC+DPF setups at 50% loading condition exhibited a reduction of 0.015 and 0.002 in CO emission.The CO emissions were also determined to be 0.116% and 0.077% higher for the SCR system, lower for the DOC+DPF configuration, and 0.109% lower for the conventional engine design.The implementation of SCR and DOC+DPF yielded a clear reduction in the concentration of CO emissions.An increase in oxygen content at higher mixes greatly reduced the production of CO.However, when powered at full capacity, carbon monoxide emissions increased for all samples because of the substantial fuel consumption required to meet the growing energy demand.The concentration of CO emissions generated during experiments is shown in Figure 3 at different loads.
Carbon Dioxide (CO2) Emissions

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the primary byproduct of hydrocarbon combustion.Many factors influence its production, including the C/H ratio, degree of unsaturation, fuel type, and cylinder temperature.Without selective catalytic reduction (SCR), with SCR, and with DOC+DPF configurations, the carbon dioxide (CO2) emittance fell by 1.44, 1.41, and 1.23%, respectively.However, a small rise of 1.5% was observed under idle loading conditions.In engines operating at 25% load, a reduction in SCR and DOC+DPF was observed, with decreases of 4.14% and 4.18%, respectively, compared to the typical levels under half-loading circumstances.

Furthermore, the increased oxygen content and viscosity rate, which allow for thorough combustion during the power stroke, contribute to the elevated concentration of CO2 emissions when the system is fully loaded.Furthermore, the increase in CO2 emissions resulted in a reduction in the concentration of detrimental CO emissions.The experimental results shown in Figures 4 and 5 depict the HC and CO2 emission concentrations at different loads.
Nitrogen Oxide (NOx) Emissions

The peak engine temperature regulates the NOx concentration, which increases with higher exhaust nitrogen (CN) levels, increased oxygen content, and longer residence durations.Under normal operating conditions, the NOx emissions for SCR and DOC+DPF in a typical engine were reduced by 56, 62, and 85 ppm, respectively.SCR decreased NOx emission due to the urea vapour injection, which reduced NOx emission.Compared to a typical diesel engine running at 50% capacity, SCR and DOC+DPF produce NOx emissions of 528 ppm and 537 ppm lower, respectively.These findings indicate that under full loading conditions, the NOx emission was lower than that of a conventional engine (968 ppm for SCR and 961 ppm for DOC+DPF configuration).While it is well recognised that higher loading rates lead to increased NOx rates, the experiment revealed lower NOx concentrations when injecting a greater amount of urea vapour.Figures 6 and 7 show the O2 and NOx emission concentrations achieved at different loads in the conducted tests.
Steady State Conditions

This image compares test results obtained during steady-state operation with various loads and test procedures.A comparative analysis of the efficacy of urea dose and NOx conversion is shown in the following evaluations.Experimental evidence has shown that the gaseous urea method greatly enhances the elimination of NOx across almost the whole range of the cycle.An essential aspect of the gas phase idea was the temperature of the urea-water solution (UWS), which was precisely monitored at the outflow of the heat chamber.The temperature of the UWS (Ultra-Water System) fell consistently due to the progressive refreshment of the urea flow by the heating chamber at each test stage.Conversely, the heating capacity provided to the chamber was consistently maintained.A key element of the gas phase concept was the urea-water solution (UWS) temperature measured at the heat chamber's outflow.The carbon monoxide (CO) emission from the gaseous urea solution was somewhat greater.
Transient Conditions

The investigation included the verification of the concept system under transient situations.The emissions of NOx were 18% reduced in the gaseous urea system, while the emissions of CO2 and NH3 were identically increased.The NH3 slip was quantified at elevated gas temperature  during the latter phase of the experimental run.A greater concentration of NH3 was observed in the gaseous urea technique.According to these test results, using the gas urea technique has been favourable in reducing NOx emissions but detrimental in reducing CO2 and NH3 emissions.
Conclusions

This study demonstrates that treating heavy-duty diesel engines with SCR exhaust effectively reduces NOx emissions to comply with national pollution regulations.However, the primary objective of SCR technologies is to incorporate them into a diesel engine that relies on constantly changing boundaries and more complex factors for optimal performance.Higherquality data on NOx selective catalytic reduction (SCR) emissions from remote investigations has been acquired.Additional development efforts are required during the SCR process, especially in engine heating and idle operating circumstances.Under inadequate chemical decomposition into ammonia and limited evaporation, injecting urea at low exhaust gas temperatures becomes necessary.This study aimed to investigate the impact of water urea solution on the transformation of NOx into the SCR catalyst.Before application upstream of the SCR catalyst, urea must undergo heating and evaporation.Enhancing the urea-thermal breakdown rate and thus reducing urea use were the objectives of improving the NOx performance.

The study also designed, constructed, and verified a bespoke gas-urea system.Despite its ease of production, the study convincingly demonstrated the advantages of urea vaporization.The gaseous urea dosage method, in contrast to the conventional urea dosage, showed a significant enhancement in the conversion of NOx to the SCR catalyst.The CO and CO2 is lowered about 0.109%, 4.18%, respectively.The emissions of NOx were 18% reduced in the gaseous urea system, while the emissions of CO2 and NH3 were identically increased.SCR and DOC+DPF produce NOx emissions of 528 ppm and 537 ppm lower, respectively.However, the study emphasizes the need for further investigation to understand the impact of the machinery fluid rate on the characteristics of the SCR machine diesel engine and the exhaust pressure-back delivery at different urea solution temperatures.It also underscores the importance of considering the different requirements for ammonia catalyst energy production.
